title: Evaluation methods, testing standards, and simulation techniques of sound absorption capabilities of cementitious materials: A review
review_question: To explore the significance and capabilities of cementitious materials in sound absorption, highlighting their role in addressing noise pollution, and to review various methods, testing standards, and simulation techniques for evaluating their sound absorption properties.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly stated, but focuses on cementitious materials, sound absorption measurement techniques, acoustic simulation, and related challenges.

synthesis_conclusions: The selection of sound absorption measurement methods (reverberation chamber, impedance tube, in-situ surface impedance) depends on material characteristics and context, requiring a customized approach and metrics like NRC, SAA, or SAAR for accurate evaluation.

Modification of concrete with materials like crumb rubber, bottom ash, and lightweight aggregates significantly enhances sound absorption properties, with specific dosages (e.g., 30% crumb rubber, up to 40% cenospheres) showing optimal performance.

Optimal acoustic performance of construction materials relies on balancing density, porosity, and surface area, achieved through careful consideration of lightweight aggregates, pore-forming agents, and water-to-cement ratios.

Frequency analysis is crucial across diverse domains (road vehicles: 20-100 Hz; railways: 20 Hz-2 kHz; aircraft: 50 Hz-10 kHz; room acoustics: 50 Hz-10 kHz, with speech 50-4 kHz and music 20-16 kHz) due to impacts on human comfort and health.

Theoretical models (Delany-Bazley-Miki, Johnson-Champoux-Allard-Lafarge) offer trade-offs between simplicity and accuracy in analyzing sound absorption in porous materials, with model selection depending on available parameters and desired precision.

Acoustic simulation methods (ODEON, CATT-Acoustics, COMSOL, ANSYS Acoustics) show considerable variation and discrepancies (up to 20% in RT, 6.6% in material studies) between simulation and experimental results, highlighting the diversity and precision of applications.

While cementitious materials show promise for sound absorption, they face challenges including increased costs (10–30%), reduced durability (up to 25-30% less longevity, 10-30% lower strength), and significant environmental impacts (7-8% global CO2 emissions, increased water usage, production waste). Addressing these requires a balanced, collaborative, and sustainable approach.
evidence_gaps: Addressing challenges related to cost, reduced durability, and environmental impact of modified cementitious materials through collaborative research and a balanced approach.
Developing solutions that are not only effective but also sustainable and practical in the face of the complexities of modern urban life.
Further research to optimize cementitious materials for cost-effectiveness, longevity, and sustainability in absorption applications.
limitations: The diffuse sound field method (reverberation chamber) integrates absorption over all angles of incidence, while the normal incidence method (impedance tube) measures absorption at a single angle, leading to discrepancies in reported absorption coefficients.
The finite-size sample effect can lead to higher absorption coefficients in the diffuse field method due to diffraction around edges, especially for small samples in large, highly reflective rooms.
The impedance tube method cannot accurately measure non-locally responding materials and requires core samples, which can alter sound absorption values.
Acoustic simulations are not 100% accurate and discrepancies can occur when compared with experimental results, especially for low-frequency ranges due to diffraction and scattering.
The production of specialized forms of concrete (e.g., pervious concrete) often leads to increased costs (10-30%) compared to traditional concrete.

Modifications to cementitious materials to enhance sound absorption can compromise their durability, leading to increased susceptibility to wear and tear, vulnerability to weathering (e.g., freeze-thaw cycles), and reduced structural integrity (10-30% lower compressive strength).

Increased porosity in cementitious materials can lead to a reduction in durability of up to 25% in regions with seasonal temperature shifts or frequent freeze-thaw cycles, necessitating premature repair/replacement and increasing lifecycle costs.
Porous materials may encounter biological hazards (mold/mildew growth) in high humidity or poor ventilation conditions.
Chemical degradation from factors like road salt or acid rain can further decrease the sound absorption efficiency and structural integrity of porous materials by 10-20%.
The production and utilization of cement-based materials raise environmental concerns, including habitat loss (1-2 km²/site) and biodiversity decrease (5-10%) from limestone extraction.
The cement industry contributes 7-8% of global CO2 emissions, with additional processing for acoustic enhancement potentially increasing emissions by 10-15%.
The cement industry consumes 9% or more of global industrial water withdrawals, and modifying cement can increase water consumption by 5-10%, exacerbating water scarcity.
